paper_title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $π_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $π_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.

sections.content: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models Khuyen Pham1, Tran Nguyen Le2, Edoardo Fazzari1, Cesare Stefanini1 Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as π0.5, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of π0.5, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated tokenlevel cross-attention, MambaAct uses lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses 10 smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https: //github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct. I. INTRODUCTION Recent flow-matching VLAs such as π0 [1] and π0.5 [2] achieve strong manipulation performance, but their iterative action-generation process introduces substantial inference cost. At every policy query, the visual-language prefix can be computed once, whereas the action expert must be evaluated repeatedly across multiple flow-matching denoising steps. As result, action generation can become the dominant source of latency even when the visual-language backbone itself is relatively compact. Recent efforts to improve VLA efficiency have largely reduced this cost by decreasing the number of sampling steps, compressing or pruning pretrained networks, reducing visualtoken processing, or redesigning the policy around smaller these approaches primarily architectures. While effective, accelerate inference by reducing how often existing components are evaluated or by simplifying the visual-language pathway and overall model. In contrast, the architecture of the repeatedly evaluated action expert itself remains comparatively underexplored as an efficiency axis. This motivates us to ask whether flow-matching inference can instead be accelerated by replacing the action-generation module while preserving the pretrained visual-language representations and standard flow-matching formulation. Corresponding author: edoardo.fazzari@mbzuai.ac.ae; 1 MBZUAI; Technical University of Denmark. We address this question with MambaAct, compact Mamba [3] action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained π0.5 visual-language encoder and replaces its large Transformer-based action expert with lightweight Mamba sequence mixer. Mamba is attractive in this setting because its selective state-space formulation provides compact inductive bias for modeling ordered, strongly correlated action sequences. As we show empirically, this design enables aggressive actionexpert compression while preserving policy performance. To efficiently condition the newly initialized expert on the pretrained VLM, we introduce Context Compressor and gated FiLM [4] interface that transform the visual-language prefix into compact representation reused throughout flowmatching denoising. The resulting expert contains only 29.7M parameters, compared with 311.5M for the original π0.5 action expert. Our main contributions are: We introduce MambaAct, establishing action-expert replacement as complementary efficiency axis for flowmatching VLAs. MambaAct replaces the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with compact Mamba expert while retaining the pretrained visuallanguage backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, without additional pretraining or distillation. We show that Mamba enables aggressive action-expert compression: MambaAct uses over 10 fewer actionexpert parameters than π0.5 while improving mean LIBERO [5] success by 1.08 percentage points across three fine-tuning seeds. Through controlled ablations, we examine the contributions of the Mamba action mixer and conditioning interface to the efficiency-performance trade-off. We further demonstrate that MambaAct composes with VLM-depth indicating reduction and transfers to SmolVLA [6], that action-expert replacement generalizes across flowmatching VLA backbones. II. RELATED WORK A. Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models The growing computational cost of VLA models has motivated range of approaches that reduce inference cost at different stages of the policy. One direction focuses on accelerating iterative action generation. SnapFlow [7], for example, uses progressive self-distillation to compress iterative flow matching into single action-expert evaluation, thereby reducing the number of sampling steps required at inference time. Complementary approaches instead reduce the cost of each network evaluation by simplifying the underlying architecture. Shallow-π [8] distills shallower visuallanguage and action transformers, while CLP [9] identifies and removes redundant layers from pretrained VLA models. Another line of work targets the visual-language pathway, where long visual-token sequences can dominate computation. General VLM pruning methods such as FastV [10] and DivPrune [11] preserve early visual processing while removing redundant tokens before later transformer layers, and have subsequently been evaluated in VLA policies [9]. VLA-specific methods further adapt this idea to robotic control: LightVLA [12], ADP [13], and SpecPrune-VLA [14] selectively reduce visual tokens while retaining task-relevant information for action prediction. Beyond pruning individual components, several works pursue efficiency through compact architectures or coordinated reductions across multiple computational axes. SmolVLA [6] reduces the overall model scale, whereas CogVLA [15] combines instructiontoken sparsification, and conditioned visual aggregation, redesigned action decoder. Similarly, EfficientVLA [16] combines token and layer reduction with feature reuse across action-generation steps. MambaAct targets different design point: it retains the pretrained π0.5 backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, but replaces the transformer action expert with compact Mamba-based expert trained jointly during task fine-tuning, without teacher models, distillation objectives, or additional pretraining. B. Mamba in Vision-Language-Action Models Mamba [3] replaces pairwise self-attention with selective state-space recurrence, providing compact mechanism for modeling ordered sequences. This makes it attractive for repeatedly evaluated action experts operating under tight parameter budgets. Mamba has been explored across sequence modeling and computer vision [17], with recent extensions to robotic perception and control [18], [19], [20]. Within VLA modeling, RoboMamba [18] uses Mamba primarily as the multimodal visual-language reasoning backbone, targeting efficient perception and reasoning rather than dense continuous action generation. Mamba has also been explored for continuous control. Mamba Policy [19] applies Mamba to continuous-action diffusion, demonstrating selective state-space models as compact action-denoising networks. However, it is not designed as an action expert conditioned on representations from pretrained vision-language backbone. More recently, SUREFlow [20] develops lightweight Mamba-based multimodal policy with uncertainty-aware residual flow matching, jointly predicting action velocity and uncertainty to selectively refine unreliable actions. Unlike MambaAct, SUREFlow constructs compact end-to-end multimodal policy rather than preserving pretrained foundation VLM and replacing only its action expert. MambaAct targets this complementary setting: accelerating the action-generation pathway of pretrained flowmatching VLA while preserving its learned visual-language representations. It retains the π0.5 VLM and standard flowmatching objective, while replacing only the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with compact Mamba expert conditioned through compressed VLM context and gated FiLM modulation. We further show that this actionexpert replacement transfers to SmolVLA. III. Experimental Setup We evaluate whether replacing the transformer-based action expert with lightweight Mamba action expert can preserve or improve policy performance while reducing inference cost. We use LIBERO to measure simulated task performance and latency, LIBERO-Plus to assess zero-shot robustness, and two real-world UR5 tasks - tube placing and nut pouring - to evaluate physical manipulation performance and deployment efficiency. Fig. 2: MambaAct architecture. MambaAct retains and jointly fine-tunes the pretrained π0.5 visual-language backbone while replacing its Transformer action expert with compact Mamba-3 expert. The VLM prefix is compressed into visual, language, and learned-query global context tokens and pooled into z, which block-specific FiLM MLPs map to scale, shift, and residual-gate parameters. The noisy action chunk Xt is projected into the initial action-token sequence H(0), while the embedded flow time ct is injected through block-specific projections. The = 4 gated Mamba-3 blocks transform the full action-token sequence into H(L), and final RMSNorm-linear head predicts the flow velocity ˆVθ. Repeated Euler updates use this velocity to obtain the denoised action chunk X0. a) Base policy and model configuration: We use OpenPI π0.5 [2] as both the base model and the controlled baseline. MambaAct the pretrained PaliGemma VLM backbone [21] including SigLIP vision encoder and Gemma visual-language prefix encoder, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with lightweight Mamba action expert. retains All π0.5-based variants are initialized from the same base checkpoint and fine-tuned using single-stage full-model recipe, in which the vision encoder, executed VLM layers, context-compression module, and action expert are optimized jointly. The MambaAct model executes all 18 VLM layers and uses four-block Mamba action expert with width 512, state size 64, expansion factor 1, and head dimension 64. The Context Compressor produces = 64 context tokens, comprising 44 visual tokens, 16 language tokens, and 4 learned-query global summary tokens. b) Training protocol: All π0.5-based policies are trained for 30,000 optimizer steps with batch size 16 and gradient accumulation 1. For the main LIBERO comparison, we independently fine-tune MambaAct and the matched π0.5 baseline with training seeds {17, 27, 42}. All other π0.5based experiments use seed 42 unless otherwise stated. We fine-tune the full VLM backbone together with the full action expert, without freezing either component. We use AdamW with gradient clipping at 1.0, weight decay 1010, and cosine learning-rate schedule from 5 105 to 5 106 without warmup. Training uses bfloat16 precision, gradient checkpointing, eight CPU workers, and single NVIDIA H100 GPU. c) Simulation benchmarks: We evaluate each policy on the standard LIBERO benchmark [5], including the SPATIAL, OBJECT, GOAL, and LIBERO-10 (later denoted as L-10) suites. Each suite contains ten tasks. We run 50 trials per task using evaluation seed 7 and report the success rate for each suite together with the unweighted average across all four suites. LIBERO inference uses image resolution 224 224, action horizon = 10, ten flow-matching denoising steps, and replanning every five environment steps. For the main LIBERO comparison, we report mean and standard deviation across these three fine-tuning seeds. However, standard LIBERO performance may mask overfitting to benchmark-specific visual and environmental conditions, as policies can degrade under small perturbations. We therefore evaluate MambaAct and the matched π0.5 baseline on LIBERO-Plus [22], which contains 10,030 test-only task instances across seven perturbation categories: CAMERA, ROBOT, LANGUAGE, LIGHT, BACKGROUND, NOISE, and LAYOUT. Following the official protocol, we run one rollout per task instance using fixed evaluation seed and report category-level and overall success rates. d) Real-world benchmarks: Our setup uses two UR5 robots  (Fig. 3)  : the left robot performs manipulation and carries wrist-mounted RealSense camera, while the right robot remains fixed and carries second RealSense camera providing the third-person view. We use third-person and wrist-mounted RGB observations at 30 fps and 640 480, resized to 224 224 with aspect-ratio-preserving padding. Object positions lie on 1010 cm grid, with blue locations used for training and in-distribution (ID) evaluation and red locations reserved for out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. For each task, we collect 112 demonstrations from 28 training configurations, with four episodes per configuration, and evaluate on 28 ID and 52 OOD trials. We consider two real-world tasks: Tube Placing and Nut transfers tube from the robot Pouring. In the former, source holder to target holder; training uses source positions A1-A2, target positions B1-B7, and two tube slots, while OOD evaluation introduces unseen source positions A3-A4 and target positions B8-B10. In the latter, the robot first places the black container on the target, then grasps the blue container and pours its contents into the black container. Training uses blue-container positions A1-A2, black-container positions B1-B7, and targets C1-C2, while OOD evaluation uses unseen blue-container positions A3-A4 and black-container positions B8-B10. For real-world evaluation, we use normalized success rate with partial credit for meaningful intermediate completion. For tube placing, trial receives 1 for successful placement, 0.5 when the tube is grasped but not inserted into the target holder, and 0 when grasping fails. For nut pouring, trial receives 1 for successful pouring, 0.5 when the black container is successfully placed but pouring fails, and 0 when the preceding grasp-and-place stage fails. e) Real-world inference: For physical deployment, the policies predict delta-joint action chunks with horizon = 50 from the visual-language observation. At each policy query, the robot executes the first 30 predicted actions at control frequency of 30 Hz before replanning. Real-world inference runs on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. f) Latency measurement: We report Prefix, Denoise, and E2E (end-to-end) latency. Prefix covers visual-language encoding and context construction, Denoise covers all ten flow-matching steps, and E2E includes the full policy query with I/O, CPU-GPU transfer, serialization, communication, and scheduling overhead. Simulation and real-world latency are measured on single H100 and RTX 5090, respectively. A. Main Results IV. RESULTS 1) LIBERO: Table highlights the performance and efficiency gains of MambaAct on LIBERO. Across three independent fine-tuning seeds, MambaAct improves average success from 96.720.14% to 97.800.43% (+1.08 percentage points), while reducing the action-expert core from 311.5M to 29.7M parameters ( 90.5%). Compared with the baseline π0.5, MambaAct improves OOD success from 86.5% to 95.2% on nut pouring and from 76.9% to 82.7% on tube placing, while also reducing model size, GFLOPs, and training time. Overall, MambaAct improves real-world OOD robustness while substantially accelerating action generation. Ablation Studies We conduct three ablation studies to assess the source of gain, composability, and transferability of MambaAct. Unless otherwise stated, all ablations use fine-tuning seed of 42 and an evaluation seed of 7. Ablation 1: Architectural source of gain. We isolate the contributions of the action mixer and conditioning interface using 2 2 comparison of Mamba and Transformer mixers with gated and cross-attention conditioning (Table V). Under gated conditioning, Mamba achieves 98.4% average success, substantially outperforming the size-matched Transformer at 85.7%. The same trend holds with cross-attention (96.7% vs. 75.6%), suggesting that the Mamba action mixer is important for preserving performance under aggressive action-expert compression. Ablation 2: Composability. Here, we study whether MambaAct can compose with complementary prefix-side VLA acceleration. Efficient VLA systems can be accelerated along multiple axes, including reducing denoising steps, pruning or compressing visual tokens, truncating VLM depth, and replacing the action expert. Because MambaAct primarily reduces computation in the repeatedly evaluated action pathway, its acceleration mechanism is distinct from methods that reduce computation in the visual-language prefix. We test this composability using VLM-depth reduction as representative prefix-side acceleration. As controlled efficiencyaccuracy trade-off, we combine MambaAct with VLM-depth reduction by executing only the first 12 VLM layers instead of all 18 layers before passing the resulting context representation to the Mamba action expert. Ablation 3: Transferability. We test whether the Mamba action expert transfers beyond π0.5 by replacing SmolVLAs Transformer action expert with 4-block Mamba expert. This reduces the action-expert size from 98.25M to 64.31M parameters, 34.5% reduction. Table VIII shows that MambaAct transfers effectively to SmolVLA. The published SmolVLA score of 87.3% in Table II uses the papers 100k-step training setting, whereas the released LIBERO checkpoint was trained for 25k steps with batch size 32. For fair comparison, we therefore reevaluate the released checkpoint under our protocol of 50 trials per task with evaluation seed 7, obtaining 81.30% average success. Under the same 25k-step, batch-32, seed1000 training budget, SmolVLA-MambaAct reaches 84.95% (+3.65 percentage points), while reducing denoising latency by 63.3% and E2E latency by 52.0%. The largest gains occur on LIBERO-10 (70.2% 77.8%) and SPATIAL (76.6% 82.6%). These results indicate that the Mamba action-expert replacement transfers beyond the π-family, reducing actionexpert size while improving average task success on second flow-matching VLA backbone. In summary, the ablations support three observations. First, Mamba substantially outperforms size-matched Transformer mixers under both evaluated conditioning interfaces, suggesting that the action mixer itself is important for preserving performance under aggressive expert compression. Second, gated conditioning provides an efficient interface between the pretrained VLM and the newly initialized action expert, although its accuracy advantage over cross-attention is partially confounded by model capacity. Third, the resulting Mamba action expert remains effective under VLM-depth reduction and transfers to second flow-matching VLA architecture. these results are consistent with benefits from Together, selective action sequence modeling and lightweight visuallanguage conditioning beyond compression alone. V. CONCLUSION We present and publicly release MambaAct, lightweight Mamba-based action expert tailored for flow-matching vision-language-action models. Rather than altering the pretrained vision-language backbone or truncating denoising steps, MambaAct directly optimizes the frequently evaluated action-generation pathway. By substituting the Transformer in π0.5 with Mamba mixer, MambaAct action expert enables aggressive compression of the repeatedly evaluated action pathway, reducing the core action-expert parameter count from 311.5M to 29.7M ( 10) while substantially lowering denoising latency. Crucially, this compression improves mean LIBERO performance across three independent fine-tuning seeds, while retaining strong robustness on LIBERO-Plus and on real-world robotic tasks. Furthermore, MambaAct seamlessly integrates with VLM-depth reduction and generalizes effectively when transferred to SmolVLA. Despite these strengths, several limitations remain. First, our real-world experiments are currently restricted to two UR5 tasks under primary spatial distribution shifts. In addition, while MambaAct composes with VLM-depth reduction, its compatibility with other efficiency techniques, such as visual-token pruning and denoising-step compression, remains to be evaluated. We also leave deeper analysis of the gated visual-language conditioning and selective Mamba state dynamics to future work. REFERENCES [1] K. Black, N. Brown, D. Driess, A. Esmail, M. Equi, C.
